articles.title: In 2020, a Michigan medical student solved a poem and found a chest hidden somewhere in Wyoming for a decade; its 476 items later sold for over $1.3 million
articles.summary: US News: A Michigan medical student solved a decade-long treasure hunt, revealing a hidden chest filled with gold and jewels worth over $1.3 million. Discover the story behind Forrest Fenn's legendary hunt, the risks taken by treasure seekers, and the significant auction that followed.
articles.body: For almost ten years, a bronze box filled with gold and jewelry was buried somewhere in the Rocky Mountains, drawing an estimated 350,000 hunters, according to Heritage Auctions, to roam through the mountains and canyons of America. Forrest Fenn, an art dealer in Santa Fe, hid the treasure in 2010 and published his memoir, The Thrill of the Chase, the same year, launching the hunt. The memoir contained a poem made up of 24 lines and nine clues. According to Fenn, the motivation behind the hiding of the chest was his diagnosis with kidney cancer in 1988, which appeared to be fatal initially but turned out to be nonfatal. The author finally hid the chest in 2010 and published his memoir during the same year so as to cheer people up after the Great Recession.A Michigan medical student located the chest in 2020According to Daniel Barbarisi's December 7, 2020, article in Outside magazine, "The Man Who Found Forrest Fenn's Treasure," the search ended in June 2020 when Jonathan "Jack" Stuef, a 32-year-old medical student from Michigan, found the chest after decoding the clues in Forrest Fenn's poem. The man discovered the poem in 2018 on Twitter and got obsessed with it to such an extent that he admitted that he was thinking about the poem for hours every day. CBS News Colorado (2022) states that Jack Stuef communicated with Forrest Fenn after locating the chest in June 2020. In the months preceding his death in September 2020, Forrest Fenn publicly disclosed that the treasure was found. Stuef's identity remained confidential for six months. According to court filings, he came forward in December 2020 after a U.S. District Court ruling required Fenn's estate to disclose his name and address as part of a lawsuit filed by attorney Barbara Andersen.The poem was kept in Fenn's self-published memoir for ten years before anyone could break it, and the sheer volume of the reaction it received became the focus of academic research later on. Psychologist Alan King of the University of North Dakota built a survey of people connected to the hunt and published his findings in Treasure Hunting as an American Subculture: The Thrill of the Chase, in the journal Human Arenas. Based on survey responses from a sample of chase participants, King's study estimated that approximately two million American adults had some association with the hunt, of whom an estimated 433,013 were experienced, competitive searchers. Furthermore, the study revealed that 80% of a well-experienced sample of 249 chasers regarded Fenn and the treasure hunt highly, whereas approximately 10% thought that the chase may turn out to be an addiction for them.The search cost some searchers far more than moneyIndeed, there were many risks involved. CBS News reported that at least four people died while searching for Forrest Fenn's treasure chest. CBS News also reported that a man was arrested after digging up graves in Yellowstone National Park while trying to find the treasure chest. Local officials in Wyoming and Montana always commented on the difficulties associated with rescue operations when searchers took marked paths but kept it a secret from everyone, including their families. As reported by ABC News (July 2017), the New Mexico State Police Chief, Pete Kassetas, officially requested that Forrest Fenn end his treasure search due to a death incident involving a Colorado pastor looking for the treasure. Fenn ignored the request, as he said that the treasure was indeed real.This subculture has created a community of devoted bloggers who would analyze every word of Fenn's poem in order to determine its true meaning. In one of his papers, The Pursuit of Unattainable Goals, published in Possibility Studies & Society, King returned to the same case to build out what he called liminal commitment theory, a framework for understanding why people commit years of their lives to goals that are, by most objective measures, extremely unlikely to be reached. As per the authors, liminality refers to the process of change of identity, which occurs over time through rites of passage. King's theory of liminal commitment builds on the Fenn case as an example, arguing that just as there are alluring aspects to being a treasure hunter, similar motivations may drive people to pursue other unattainable ventures. Unattainability refers to the distance of the goal from the subject and low levels of perceived attainability.The auction sold 476 lots from the collectionIn an article released by Heritage Auctions titled “Heritage Auctions Opens Forrest Fenn’s Treasure Chest to Collectors”, dated September 19, 2022, the recovered treasure chest and all the objects contained therein were sold to Tesouro Sagrado Holdings, LLC, a private buyer. According to Heritage Auctions, Jack Stuef did not disclose the sale price. During December of that year, the new owner enlisted the services of Heritage Auctions in Dallas for the sale of 476 items in an online auction spanning one month. The owner retained a portion of the chest's original contents, which were excluded from the sale; the remaining 476 lots went to auction. At the close of bidding, all 476 lots sold, with 1,643 bidders participating and a total of $1,307,946 generated.The item that sold at the highest price was an Alaskan gold nugget weighing 549 grams, roughly the weight of nine to eleven large eggs and fetching a sum of $55,200. The second highest-priced item in the collection was a little wax-sealed glass jar alleged to contain a 20,000-word autobiography written in micro-text and placed in the chest by Fenn. As he revealed in his autobiography, Fenn included the story to ensure that whoever discovered the treasure would also learn something about him, the man who had hidden it.A hunt that outlived its own mysteryThe precise location of the chest was never officially revealed by Fenn, and even Stuef has kept it to himself, only mentioning that it was somewhere in Wyoming. However, some participants of the treasure hunt have speculated that the chest may have been located somewhere in Yellowstone National Park. What Heritage Auctions and King's research confirm is the scale of the phenomenon: a self-published poem drew hundreds of thousands of people into the hunt, and the treasure was eventually found years later.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Georgia city moved a pre-Civil War house out of the way of a hotel project instead of demolishing it; after a $500,000 relocation and restoration, it is becoming a coffee shop
articles.summary: US News: A house that survived for more than a century is getting a new life not as a museum, but as a place for coffee and community. In Acworth, Georgia, the.
articles.body: A house that survived for more than a century is getting a new life not as a museum, but as a place for coffee and community. In Acworth, Georgia, the historic McCray House was moved from its original site to make way for a new hotel, rather than being demolished. The nearly $500,000 relocation and restoration effort has preserved the pre-Civil War structure, which is now being prepared as a new location for Bizarre Coffee. According to Bizarre Coffee's official Acworth page, the company's forthcoming shop will operate inside the historic McCray House at 4415 Cherokee Street, next to Logan Farm Park.A historic house gets a second chanceThe McCray House dates to the mid-1800s and is one of Acworth's surviving historic structures. The house later became closely associated with the McCray family, who acquired it in the 1960s. Over the years, the property became part of the community's social life, with family events, weddings, holiday celebrations and a petting zoo among the memories associated with the home. When redevelopment was planned for the property's original location, the city chose to relocate the structure instead of allowing it to be lost. CBS Atlanta reported in March 2026 that a new hotel was being developed on the original lot and that the city spent $500,000 to move the house and repurpose it as a coffee shop.The City of Acworth purchased the abandoned 19th-century property and approximately three acres in 2021. Earlier plans involved transferring the house to Cobb Landmarks for restoration and use as an event and exhibit space, but the nonprofit eventually stepped away from the proposal because of budget considerations. In 2025, the city's Board of Aldermen approved $84,800 for architectural and engineering services connected with the relocation.Moving the house instead of tearing it downRelocating a historic house is far more complicated than simply transporting a building from one address to another. According to CROFT & Associates, which worked with the City of Acworth and Macallan Construction, the McCray Farmhouse was separated from later additions, placed on steel beams and transported along Cherokee Street to its new location at the entrance to Logan Farm Park.The move was part of a wider effort to preserve the building's historic character while giving it a practical future. The City of Acworth's project updates also linked the relocation to plans for a new hotel on the property's original site. Jeff Chase, Acworth's director of downtown development, tourism and historic preservation, told CBS Atlanta how the new foundation was prepared. Chase said the structure was positioned over a cinder-block wall, with the wall then being built upward to meet the bottom of the house.For members of the McCray family, the project also represented the preservation of decades of personal memories. Speaking to CBS Atlanta, Moose McCray recalled the house's connection to weddings, children and community gatherings and said he was glad that the property would be preserved.From family home to coffee shopThe next chapter for the building is considerably different from its earlier roles. Bizarre Coffee is preparing to open its Acworth location inside the restored McCray House. The company's official website currently lists the location as "coming soon" at 4415 Cherokee Street and describes it as a historic home that has been part of the Acworth community for generations. Bizarre Coffee also says the future shop will sit beside Logan Farm Park, include an outdoor patio, and retain much of the historic house's character. The company has described the project as the next chapter for the building as it prepares to become its Acworth location.The City of Acworth celebrated the restoration with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on July 16, 2026. The city said the project team had worked to maintain the historic integrity of the building while allowing its story to continue through a new use. The City of Acworth also noted that Sabrina Kaylor, owner of Bizarre Coffee, would bring new memories to the property when the shop opens. The restoration work has included attention to the building's exterior and interior character. Macallan Construction, one of the project's partners, said the work included a new roof, exterior siding, refinished floors and restoration of intricate porch details as the house was prepared for its new use as Bizarre Coffee.A preserved landmark with a new purposeThe McCray House is therefore becoming an unusual example of adaptive reuse. Instead of remaining an abandoned structure or disappearing beneath redevelopment, the historic house has been physically moved, restored and given a commercial purpose. Its future as a coffee shop also means the building will remain part of everyday life in Acworth. Visitors will be able to use a structure that dates back to the mid-19th century while experiencing a completely different chapter of its history.For a house that has already passed through multiple generations, survived major changes around it and moved to a new location, its next chapter will begin with something much simpler: coffee, conversation and another generation of community memories.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, BSEE reported 43 retired Gulf platforms had joined Rigs-to-Reefs since 2017, providing habitat where more than 100 fish species live
articles.summary: US News: The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) reveals that 43 decommissioned platforms in the Gulf of Mexico have been successfully transformed into artificial reefs, fostering a vibrant marine ecosystem and supporting over 100 fish species since 2017.
articles.body: Hundreds of aging oil and gas rigs in the Gulf of Mexico are decommissioned each year. While federal regulations demand that these rigs be dismantled once they are no longer operational, more and more rigs are now being left behind to serve as artificial reefs where sea life can flourish after the drilling process is over. The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), the federal agency that regulates offshore oil and gas operations, reported that 43 retired platforms had been converted into artificial reefs between 2017 and 2020 through its Rigs-to-Reefs program. That brought the total number of converted structures in the Gulf past 500. These aren't temporary fixes. Once a jacket's drilling days are over, toppling its steel lattice structure in place, or partially submerging it, turns it into a permanent underwater habitat.The statistics presented by BSEE also reveal the reasons why states are always opting for this particular choice instead of the complete removal of the platforms. Over 100 species of fish have been identified around these platforms, and many of these are significant in commercial and recreational angling. These structures provide a surface for algae, sponges, individual coral colonies, and various other invertebrates to thrive on.California research measured record fish production on platform structuresThe reasons behind their effectiveness are not only anecdotal. In a 2014 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Jeremy Claisse of Occidental College and colleagues reported that California oil platforms had the highest secondary fish production per unit of seafloor area of any marine habitat studied to date, about an order of magnitude higher than other marine ecosystems, including estuaries, traditionally considered among the most productive on the planet. The researchers analyzed four Southern California platforms using hydroacoustics and trawls over 18 months, then converted the fish biomass they measured into standing stock and annual production per square meter of seafloor. Drawing on separate visual surveys of 16 platforms conducted over as long as 15 years by co-authors Milton Love and Ann Bull, the team estimated that platform fish communities produced roughly ten times more biomass than other marine habitats studied, with the platforms' midwater structure accounting for most of that production; the researchers attributed this largely to rockfish larvae settling and maturing on the platforms' hard vertical surfaces. The same paper found that, compared specifically to nearby natural rocky reefs at similar depths, the platforms produced more than 27 times as much fish biomass.This is significant in terms of the Gulf, because structures in the Gulf are more homogeneous despite being different from the environment in California. An eight-leg structure in the Gulf, for example, may support 12,000 to 14,000 fish at one time, according to the Coastal Marine Institute at Louisiana State University.Louisiana survey found the same pattern at a converted platform reefThis finding inevitably led to a natural inquiry: Is this true for the Gulf of Mexico, which has many more platforms than the California coast? According to the Bulletin of Marine Science, the study conducted by Kevin Boswell et al. investigated Freeport Sulphur Mine Artificial Reef, a platform turned into an artificial reef off the coast of Louisiana, which was the biggest reef structure in the northern Gulf of Mexico at the time. It was determined through the use of mobile acoustic sampling that there was five times less biomass and fish density at 10 metres and 16 times less at 30 metres from the reef structure. The Bulletin of Marine Science research also found that fish concentrated most heavily near the bottom of the water column rather than near the surface, a pattern that has practical implications for how platforms are toppled or partially removed during conversion.In combination, these two studies account for the biological principle behind BSEE's estimate of 43 platforms. As the research above suggests, the platforms' complex structure, not simple attraction, appears to be what drives the high fish production observed around them.Reefing costs less than full platform removalNone of this implies that choosing between removal and reefing is a straightforward task. By keeping the jacket in situ rather than hauling it to shore for disposal, companies reduce their costs, while coastal communities receive diving and fishing opportunities that would vanish following decommissioning of the platform. Yet, from the scientific basis of the project, California production calculations through to acoustic measurements in Louisiana, it becomes apparent that the environmental benefit is not coincidental. Given that fewer than 2,000 platforms are expected to remain for decommissioning in the Gulf over the next few years, the 43 projects registered by BSEE from 2017 to 2020 may represent only a small share of future reefing projects.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From 2020 to 2023, Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste for cultch and reef-replenishment work along its Gulf Coast
articles.summary: US News: From 2020 to 2023, Mississippi launched a unique oyster-shell recycling pilot under the 'Save Our Shells' initiative, transforming restaurant waste into vital hard substrate for oyster reef restoration along its Gulf Coast. Discover the significance of this project in boosting oyster populations and maintaining marine ecosystems.
articles.body: From 2020 through 2023, the state of Mississippi ran a shell collection and recycling pilot program that redirected discarded shells from Gulf Coast restaurants and put them back into the water as cultch, which is the hard material that young oysters use to cling to in order to grow. The pilot program was conducted under the initiative “Save Our Shells,” and helped solve an issue which had gone unnoticed in the Gulf region: as the industry shifted away from centralized shucking toward selling live oysters directly to restaurants, the resulting shells became scattered across many small locations rather than concentrated at a few processing plants, leaving them a largely uncollected resource.How the funding and structure came togetherAccording to MDEQ and RESTORE Council program documentation, the Mississippi Sound Oyster Shell Recycling Program was funded with a RESTORE Act grant of approximately $650,000, drawn from civil penalty funds tied to the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and designated for Gulf Coast restoration and recovery. The funds were used for Mississippi's Oyster Shell Recycling Pilot Project to recycle oyster shells from restaurants. The department contracted The Nature Conservancy to manage the program, with the first phase spent on planning before the shell collection itself launched in 2023. After the construction process, the restaurants retain the shucked shells for reuse, where contractors come by to transport the shells to a location for exposure to sunlight for many months, thus eliminating all bacteria and organic materials in the shells before placing them in the ocean. Cultch production is then transferred to the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to use in the replenishment of the oyster reefs in coastal areas within the state.Why shell cultch matters more than most substitutesOysters require something hard to settle on, but shell is often preferred by oysters as cultch over concrete, limestone, and gravel. An article in the Marine Ecology Progress Series researched Louisiana’s Sister Lake and found that oyster biomass from reefs made using shell cultch reached 14.6 kilograms per square meter after three years, with faster shell accretion than reef subsidence. The same Marine Ecology Progress Series also noted that the reef growth trajectory was unique to each site: reefs situated less than 8 kilometres apart grew in different ways, with recruitment and mortality differing greatly across sites. Nonetheless, within just three years, all the reefs harbored high numbers of oysters averaging 728 ± 102 per square meter, and the growth of the shell exceeded the local needs to match the rates of subsidence and shell erosion.Suwannee Sound provides a parallel view from a different perspective. Oyster density was monitored over fourteen years, nine years before and five years after a massive restoration of limestone beds. The number of oysters per square meter at the newly restored sites rose from nearly zero to 91 in six months and to 244 in five years. The study, "Restoration Is a Partial But Not Complete Solution for Long-Term Declines in Oyster Populations: A Case History From the Northeastern Gulf of America," led by W.E. Pine and USGS colleagues and published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries: Dynamics, Management and Ecosystem Science, found that rebuilding hard substrate was an essential step in reef recovery, though the paper's title itself signals that restoration is only a partial, not complete, solution to long-term oyster decline.What sets Mississippi's approach apartThe project carried out in Mississippi has been somewhat different since it used a single grant that has covered its funding throughout several years instead of starting the project step-by-step in restaurants. Such an approach has allowed setting a rather high collection goal; however, it implied spending the first few years not on getting results but on planning and building the collection infrastructure. The project itself is quite consistent with the findings of the research, since the shells, which might otherwise be sent to a landfill, is now used to recreate reefs that will contribute to the process of filtering the water as well as the development of recreational and commercial fisheries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, a retired Scottish businessman thought his detector had found a spoon, then uncovered 100-plus Viking treasures; the hoard was acquired for nearly £2 million
articles.summary: UK News: A retired Scottish businessman discovered more than 100 Viking treasures in a field in 2014, leading to a valuation of nearly £2 million for the Galloway Hoard, which offers insights into Viking trade and culture.
articles.body: A routine afternoon of metal detecting in a Scottish field turned into a major archaeological discovery when a retired businessman uncovered a buried collection of Viking-age treasures. What first looked like an old spoon turned out to be part of a hoard of gold, silver, jewellery, religious objects and rare textiles buried for more than a millennium. The discovery would eventually lead to a reward of almost £2 million for the detectorist.According to National Museums Scotland, Derek McLennan discovered the Galloway Hoard in September 2014 at Balmaghie in Kirkcudbrightshire, Dumfries and Galloway, after receiving permission to metal-detect on the land. The hoard contained more than 100 objects and was buried around AD 900. It included more than 5kg of silver, gold and other materials, with objects originating from Ireland, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and areas as far away as Asia. In 2017, the hoard was allocated to National Museums Scotland after the museum raised £1.98 million to acquire it for the nation.From a suspected spoon to a buried treasureWhen McLennan was scanning with the metal detector in the ploughed field, he got some response from the soil. When he recovered the first item, it seemed ordinary at first, but after turning it over he realised it could be linked to the Viking era. At first sight, he thought it was a silver spoon.According to The Guardian, it soon became apparent that the find was much bigger than just the one item. More than 100 items were unearthed at the site and included silver ingots and arm-rings, brooches, a gold bird-shaped pin, a gold ingot, and a highly decorated silver-gilt vessel. The silver Christian cross with its distinctive enamelled decoration shows that the find was more complex than a simple Viking treasure.The way the objects were buried added important context to the discovery. Researchers found separate bundles and caches, with objects wrapped in materials including leather and textiles. Some of these organic materials survived remarkably well, providing archaeologists with evidence about how the objects were prepared before burial. Research published in the Journal of Archaeological Science examined traces of textiles preserved in corrosion products on metal objects from the hoard. The work demonstrated how even tiny remnants of fabric can reveal information about how artefacts were wrapped and deposited.A collection with unexpected originsOne of the most striking artefacts is a rock-crystal flask set in elaborate gold. It has been established that the rock crystal was actually cut in an earlier period and was probably made in the Roman era, before it was used in the making of the later artefact. The flask had been placed in a leather bag lined with silk.An additional unique find is the presence of silk. The National Museums Scotland also states that the hoard included the earliest examples of Scottish silk along with wool and linen. These finds matter because organic artefacts rarely survive for long in archaeological hoards. This evidence cannot be gained from studying only gold and silver. The hoard also includes unusual items that complicate ideas about Viking wealth. Alongside precious metals, glass beads, crystal stones, peculiar pendants, and even soil balls with traces of gold have been found. A recent interpretation has added another clue. A runic inscription on one of the silver arm-rings has been interpreted as meaning “This is the community's property”, although researchers stress that the reading contains uncertainties. Researchers say the inscription may indicate that at least part of the hoard belonged to a community rather than a single individual.Nearly £2 million for the discoveryAccording to the National Heritage Memorial Fund, the Galloway Hoard was valued at £1.98 million in 2017, with the Queen’s and Lord Treasurer’s Remembrancer allocating it to National Museums Scotland on the condition that the museum raised the required amount. The acquisition was funded by the National Heritage Memorial Fund, the Art Fund, the Scottish Government, charitable trusts and members of the public. McLennan's discovery has since become part of a much larger research story. The objects are being examined using conservation, scientific analysis, X-rays, CT scanning and other techniques to reconstruct their individual histories and understand why they were brought together.The story has since travelled far beyond Scotland. In 2025, the Galloway Hoard was transported to Adelaide for its first overseas exhibition, forming a link with Australia, as the metal detector that McLennan was using was produced by Minelab, a company from Adelaide. What began with a detector reading and a spoon-like object turned into a treasure that had lain untouched for about 1,100 years. It offers a snapshot of movement, trade and beliefs in the Viking era.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump extends $100K H-1B visa fee until Sept 2027 but court stay remains: White House cites plunge in filings by IT cos
articles.summary: US News: In a major development especially for Indian tech professionals who constitute a fair chunk of H-1B visa holders and American sponsoring companies, US.
articles.body: In a major development especially for Indian tech professionals who constitute a fair chunk of H-1B visa holders and American sponsoring companies, US President Donald Trump has issued a fresh presidential proclamation extending the controversial $100K H-1B visa fee for another 12 months, stretching the policy through Sept 21, 2027.However, immigration attorneys emphasize that despite the White House's aggressive push, the fee remains legally blocked by a federal court order.Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm explained, “The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) remains barred from collecting the $100K H-1B fee under the Sept 2025 proclamation, which was due to expire on Sept 21, 2026. Since the new proclamation is issued as an extension, USCIS should be barred from collecting the $100K fee under the new proclamation as well. If USCIS takes the position that the new proclamation is outside of the purview of the existing court order, plaintiffs in the ongoing litigation are likely to quickly challenge that view.”Greg Siskind, co-founder at Siskind Susser, an immigration law firm pointed out that the language is virtually identical in the new proclamation, but the new version states that the fee applies to people seeking admission from outside the US (via consulates or ports of entry)—turning previous agency guidance into official proclamation text.The preamble to this proclamation explicitly states that: “Finally, my Administration continues to explore other complementary efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration program administration.”Siskind adds that this signals that the Trump administration may try to implement permanent high fees through the standard rule making process of notice-and-comment.Furthermore, sponsoring employers could also face a compounding financial squeeze from a separate proposed regulation targeting an additional $103K fee, which would not only apply to H-1Bs who were outside US and were selected in the lottery, but will also cover students from within the US who are transiting from a F-1 visa to an H-1B.Read also: US proposes $103,265 H-1B fee: Hiring set to become more costlyWexler adds, “In addition, last month, USCIS separately proposed a regulation that would impose a fee of more than $103K on all cap-subjectH-1B petitions. That fee would be separate from and in addition to the $100K H-1B proclamation fee, where applicable, if the proclamation fee were to be reinstated by further court order.”Thus, if the proclamation fee is ultimately revived by higher courts and the separate USCIS cap-subject fee rule goes into final effect, affected employers could theoretically face cumulative financial barriers totaling over $200K per petition (application) for sponsoring H-1B cap workers.Core takeaways: The Extension: The White House has extended the Sept 19, 2025 proclamation imposing a $100K fee on certain H-1B petitions through Sept 21, 2027.The Legal Status: Because the original 2025 framework was vacated by a federal district court, the extended fee policy inherits the same legal block, meaning USCIS remains barred from collecting the $100K fee for now. As was reported by TOI the US federal appeals court refused to stay a lower (district) court’s order that had struck down the controversial $100k fee on H-1B visa applications for new workers hired from outside the US. The plaintiffs in this case were 20 US states.The Compounding Threat: In addition to the proclamation fee, USCIS has separately proposed a regulation that would impose a fee of more than $103K on all cap-subject H-1B petitions—creating a potential multi-layered financial hurdle for employers.Read also: US appeals court refuses to stay order striking down Trump's $100k H-1B fee; relief for sponsoring employersKey statistics and claims from the White House proclamation:The newly released White House proclamation details several official metrics highlighting the administration's policy impacts since the original Sept 2025 order:Over 700 petitions paid: The administration reports that the $100K fee payment has been submitted for more than 700 petitions (H-1B visa applications) since its implementation in Sept 2025.92% plunge in H-1B registrations by large IT outsourcing firms: The White House credits the restrictions with a massive reduction in registrations from large IT staffing and outsourcing firms dropping from 24,946 down to just 2,055 filings, a 92% decrease.Consular requests collapse: Consular processing requests aimed at bringing overseas workers directly into the US fell by nearly 97% between the FY 2025 and FY 2027 cap seasons.Surge in beneficiaries holding a Master's degree: There has been a shift in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with registrations for beneficiaries with at least a US. Master’s degree rising from 45.1% of total registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1% for FY 2027. Further job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3% of H-1B registration selections while those corresponding with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8%.The Indian workforce connection:Indian nationals especially those in the tech sector represent the absolute backbone of the H-1B programme, making any major shifts in policy disproportionately impactful on the Indian diaspora, even as reliance on H-1B visas by Indian tech companies has significantly reduced.According to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP) only three Indian-based companies in FY 2025 were among the top 25 employers with approved H-1B petitions for initial employment. In FY 2025, the top seven Indian-based companies had only 4,573 H-1B petitions approved for initial employment, a 70% drop from FY 2015 and 37% fewer than in FY 2024.However, Indians continue to dominate the H-1B visa holders spectrum.Initial employment dominance: According to official USCIS data for the fiscal year ended Sept 30, 2025, India-born beneficiaries accounted for 50.3% (57,747 out of 114,806) of H-1B petitions approved for initial employment.Continuing employment strength: The concentration was drastically higher among renewals: India-born beneficiaries accounted for a massive 77.6% (226,359 out of 291,542) of H-1B petitions approved for continuing employment, anchoring senior engineering and tech operations across corporate America.With the White House doubling down on its high-skilled immigration overhaul even as federal courts block its path, stakeholders on both sides of the Atlantic are bracing for a prolonged legal showdown. For India’s massive tech diaspora and the corporate giants relying on their expertise, the coming months will test the limits of executive power over America's borders.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: H1-B visa price hike gets extension till September 2027: How this will impact Indian engineers, technicians and others who want to work in the US
articles.summary: Tech News News: US President Donald Trump has extended sweeping restrictions on the H-1B non-immigrant visa route for an additional twelve months, keeping a mandatory.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has extended sweeping restrictions on the H-1B non-immigrant visa route for an additional twelve months, keeping a mandatory $100,000 fee in place for specific foreign professionals, including technology workforce, looking to enter America. According to an official proclamation issued by the White House, the curbs originally implemented in September 2025 will now run through September 21, 2027. Administration officials stated the extension was required because the market conditions and alleged system abuses that triggered the initial rules continue to persist.Key details of the $100,000 ruleUnder the directive, foreign specialty occupation workers covered by the order cannot cross into the US unless their employer petitions include, or are supplemented with, a steep $100,000 payment. The payment condition hits employees situated outside the US who attempt to travel into the country after September 21, 2026.The Homeland Security Secretary retains discretionary authority to grant waivers for an individual worker, a corporate workforce, or an entire commercial sector. However, this applies solely if the employment is certified as vital to US national interests and presents no threat to domestic safety or welfare. The administration says that third-party staffing agencies and IT outsourcing providers have long manipulated the visa route to displace American personnel with cheaper offshore talent.“As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the United States, but it has been exploited to replace, not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. Certain employers, including information technology (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the system to suppress wages and displace American workers, and this has both harmed the labor market for American workers while also making it difficult to attract and retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a large volume of entry-level temporary H‑1B workers, generally at a much lower salary compared to full‑time, traditional workers, and some of these firms later outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign labor flooding the American labor market and making it difficult for American workers and recent graduates, especially in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields, to find employment.”Why Indian engineers and skilled workers face the heaviest BlowThe decision delivers a hard setback to Indian software developers, engineers and technical personnel eyeing careers in the US. Indian citizens represent the overwhelming majority of program beneficiaries, making them uniquely vulnerable to rising regulatory costs.Official US government figures from USCIS FY2025 H-1B report earlier this year show that Indian candidates secured nearly 70% of all approved H-1B petitions. China placed second by a wide margin, accounting for only 12.1% of approvals.Under the old system, companies paid just $995 per applicant, which included a $215 lottery entry fee and an employer petition charge of $780. The new annual requirement of $100,000 is a more than 10,000% increase in costs and will require corporate sponsors to rethink how they hire internationally.The rule imposes a massive financial hurdle for overseas candidates, making it prohibitively costly for American companies to hire them. Industry analysts expect corporate sponsors to pull back on applications, likely triggering a sharp decline in overall visa grants.While senior specialists possessing niche, highly technical backgrounds may still secure backing, junior talent and early-career software developers face dwindling prospects as employers reconsider the heavy upfront investment.“The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary’s discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the national interest and does not pose a threat to the security or welfare of the United States.”Last year, tech giants issued urgent travel advisories, triggering panic among foreign workers currently on leave or visiting family abroad, forcing corporate human resources teams to step in to protect their existing personnel.Major corporate employers, including Amazon, Microsoft, and JPMorgan, circulated urgent notices advising H-1B workers to remain stateside or immediately fly back to the US before the updated pricing rules take effect at midnight Saturday, September 20 2025.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.body: For decades, 2,060 acres of California’s Central Coast remained closed to the public as a buffer around the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant. Now, the land above Avila Beach in San Luis Obispo County is set to become a nature preserve with hiking trails and campsites after a $42 million conservation deal.The Wildlands Conservancy, a nonprofit land trust, has agreed to acquire the property known as Wild Cherry Canyon, San Francisco Chronicle reported. On Thursday, the state agreed to provide $42 million through the State Coastal Conservancy, allowing the organisation to proceed with the purchase.The property is owned by Eureka Energy, a subsidiary of Pacific Gas and Electric Company, which operates the nearby nuclear facility. The land has coastal hills, valleys, native grasslands and oak and pine woodlands.The land which has been the subject of development plans, including proposals for high-end homes, is on the path towards becoming public open space, after the deal. The Wildlands Conservancy plans to create trails and camping opportunities while protecting Native American cultural sites. The preserve is expected to open to the public within five years, while guided tours could begin as early as next year.Wild Cherry Canyon becomes nature preserveWild Cherry Canyon is at the southeastern end of the larger Diablo Canyon Lands, between Avila Beach and Port San Luis. Cattle currently graze on the property, while a road through the area leads to the power plant.The wider Diablo Canyon Lands cover part of the Irish Hills, with rugged cliffs above sandy beaches and tide pools. Some peaks rise to about 1,500 feet. The area also has native grasslands and oak and pine woodlands, but much of the landscape has remained inaccessible to the public.“We are excited about the opportunity to establish public access here. This scenic access is what we call absolutely world class,” said Tim Duff, project manager at the Coastal Conservancy.The three major properties around Diablo Canyon could eventually form about 12,000 acres of preserved open space. The area would extend from Montana De Oro State Park in the north to Avila Beach in the south and run along 14 miles of coastline.Local residents and officials have pushed for decades to protect the lands around the nuclear plant and make them accessible to visitors. Wild Cherry Canyon is expected to be the first of three major properties to meet the state’s conservation and public-access requirements.Five- to six-mile trail Frazier Haney, executive director of the Wildlands Conservancy, said protecting Native American cultural sites would be among the organisation’s priorities. These include sites connected to the yak tityu tityu yak tiłhini Northern Chumash Tribe.The plan is to build a five- to six-mile loop trail at Wild Cherry Canyon. The site will be the first part of an eventual 20-mile coastal trail across the Diablo Canyon Lands.“Once you get up on these hills, this is as beautiful as the California coast gets anywhere,” Haney said. “You’ll be able to go for a hike, then end your hike by going out on the pier in Port San Luis, and get something to eat and drink. It will just be a wonderful experience for people.”The conservation plan comes as the future of the Diablo Canyon nuclear plant remains under discussion. The facility had been scheduled to close in 2025, but Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Legislature decided to extend its operation because of electricity demand.The plant is now scheduled to run until 2030, although another extension is under consideration. As a condition for temporarily continuing nuclear operations, state officials required PG&E to help permanently protect the surrounding lands and eventually provide public access.Development plans delayed conservationThe acquisition follows nearly two decades of attempts to conserve Wild Cherry Canyon. Disagreements over the price and competing plans for the property had delayed earlier efforts.After the dispute was settled, the Wildlands Conservancy saw an opportunity to move forward. Under the agreement, nearly all of the $42 million will be used to buy out the lease. That is expected to be completed later this year, while the remaining money will go towards the purchase of the property, anticipated next year.“The community has been dedicated to making this happen. We just got thrown the ball in the fourth quarter of the game,” Haney said.Decades-long effort reaches major stepThe effort to protect the lands around Diablo Canyon has involved conservation groups, local residents and state officials for decades.Kaila Dettman, executive director of the Land Conservancy of San Luis Obispo County, said the organisation had been working for decades to protect the properties and secure public access.“This is a really exciting vision, and we don’t want it to slip by,” Dettman said. “It’s a special part of our county and, frankly, the state. It really gives you a sense of wild California, old California.”Kara Woodruff, a San Luis Obispo resident who helped form Friends of the Diablo Canyon Lands, said she had been thinking about Wild Cherry Canyon for more than 26 years.“The fact that this is finally coming together is the greatest news I can imagine,” Woodruff said. “I’ve been thinking about Wild Cherry Canyon for over 26 years.”John Laird helped secure funding for the deal and negotiate the requirement that PG&E conserve the properties around the nuclear complex.“There were plenty of times when it looked like it might not happen, but the Central Coast community never gave up,” Laird said in a statement Thursday. “Protecting Wild Cherry Canyon is a major step toward preserving the incredible lands surrounding Diablo Canyon for generations to come.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2001, Boston Harbor scientists released red dye to test how treated wastewater dispersed from the new outfall into Massachusetts Bay
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Boston Harbor scientists used red dye to ensure safe wastewater outfall to Massachusetts Bay, leading to a cleaner and healthier marine ecosystem.
articles.body: For most of the 20th century, Boston Harbour had a bad reputation. Decades of inadequately treated sewage from the Deer Island facility flowed directly into the harbor's shallow waters, stifling marine life and obstructing beaches, making it a national symbol of urban pollution that even made an appearance in a presidential campaign. Cleaning up the treatment plant involved more than just improving it. It involved figuring out a safer place to send the cleaned water and presenting compelling evidence that the new approach would work.In the lead up to September 2000, the MWRA was planning to stop dumping into Boston Harbour entirely and route treated effluent down a brand new outfall tunnel into Massachusetts Bay. Engineers needed to examine what would happen to that water when it exited the pipe. The simplest and most reliable solution available was dye.Follow the colour nine miles of tunnelThe treated wastewater traveled through a 9.5-mile rock tunnel beneath Massachusetts Bay before reaching 55 diffuser risers spread across the final 1.25 miles of the system, allowing the effluent to mix gradually with surrounding seawater. Hydraulic calculations had demonstrated on paper this plan would dilute the wastewater by a considerable margin before it could affect marine life or public beaches.Scientists chose a fluorescent chemical called Rhodamine WT, which has been used to trace water for years since it glows brilliantly under certain lights and is safe to people and wildlife at the concentrations involved. Researchers were able to track the plume as it passed through the diffuser system and out into open water by adding it to the effluent stream and sampling the water at various distances and depths to measure how quickly the vivid colour faded. The quicker the fading, the more potent the dilution. The measurements helped scientists evaluate the dilution and mixing performance of the new outfall after it began operating.Why a coloured plume meant so muchThis testing was massive. The project needed a federal discharge permit, and MWRA had to do field testing and show that the outfall would meet the dilution rates that earlier scale model experiments had predicted before the project could advance to full-scale operation with confidence. However, one test on a calm day would not tell the whole story. So researchers used acoustic tracking and current profiling equipment, together with dye tracing, to get a complete picture of how the plume moved and mixed with surrounding seawater under various tidal and weather circumstances.The results supported the decision to move the discharge away from the shallow waters of Boston Harbor and into deeper waters with stronger mixing and dilution. The real-world findings were remarkably in line with projections from physical-scale models developed years earlier, showing the large investment in the tunnel and diffuser system was paying off just as the engineers had hoped.A bright chapter in harbour renewalThe reversal in Boston Harbour since the outfall went on line in September 2000 is already well documented: cleaner beaches, healthier shellfish beds, and a marine ecology that continues to recover from decades of neglect. Since then, MWRA says monitoring has indicated a continuously cleaner harbour and a healthy Massachusetts Bay, as well as clean bills of health for nearby Cape Cod Bay and the Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, a feeding area for endangered right whales.That recovery would not have been possible with the same scientific certainty without the quieter, less dramatic effort that preceded it, a plume of benign red dye vanishing into the Atlantic as engineers on research ships tracked its every trace. The plume-tracking work became part of the monitoring program that followed the outfall’s opening and helped document changes in Boston Harbor and Massachusetts Bay.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1927, Henry Ford took over a stretch of the Amazon rainforest to build an American town inside it; in 1945 he was forced to sell it for $250,000
articles.summary: US News: Imagine a Midwestern town with a swimming pool, a golf course and a movie theatre located in the middle of the Amazon rainforest, several hundred kilo.
articles.body: Imagine a Midwestern town with a swimming pool, a golf course and a movie theatre located in the middle of the Amazon rainforest, several hundred kilometres upriver from anything resembling a city. While it might sound like something from a set of a movie, it's not. In 1927, Henry Ford, the legend who put America on wheels began to look for land in Brazil to build his own version of small-town Michigan in the depths of the jungle. He finally found it in 1928 and named it Fordlandia. While the town had everything one would need, what it never had, across the seventeen years of trying, was enough rubber to be worth it, as per a report by Science Blog.Why Ford wanted his own rubberRubber was the choke point of the car business. Tyres, belts, hoses, gaskets, seals: a Model A was full of the stuff, and nearly all of it came from British and Dutch plantations in Southeast Asia, grown from stock that had been carried out of Brazil in the first place. As Henry Ford’s account of the venture records, Henry Wickham took 70,000 rubber tree seedlings out of the Amazon in 1876 for cultivation in the East Indies, and Brazil lost the trade it had invented.Britain then tried to prop up the price with the Stevenson Plan in 1922. Ford, who objected to paying other people’s margins on principle, decided to cut them out.In July 1927 the Brazilian government handed him a free concession of a million hectares along the Tapajós River, on terms of seven per cent of annual profits to the federal government and two per cent to local municipalities, payable after twelve years of operation.Building a townIn August 1928, two vessels left for the Amazon carrying what amounted to a town in a kit form: tractors, prefabricated buildings, a sawmill, hospital equipment, a powerhouse, ice-making machinery and railway gear. Leading the expedition, and then running the plantation, was a Danish sea captain named Einar Oxholm, who had no agricultural experience at all.Ford’s instinct was to send factory men, on the theory that anyone who understood process could master a field outside it, so the plantation spent its early years under Ford-trained industrial staff rather than horticultural specialists.The wages were good. Workers were offered 35 cents a day plus free food, housing and medical care, against roughly 20 cents on the Asian plantations.A riot in 1930But certain rules had to be followed. Alcohol and tobacco were banned, and the dining hall served brown rice, wholemeal bread, oatmeal and canned peaches, which Ford considered healthy and his Brazilian workforce considered inedible. There were square dances and poetry readings. Work ran through the middle of the day in equatorial heat, not in the cool hours before dawn and after dusk that local labourers preferred.The workforce responded by slipping off to a settlement a few kilometres upstream that they nicknamed the Island of Innocence, which had bars, nightclubs and brothels. A manager replaced table service in the dining hall with a self-serve queue, and workers took machetes to the cafeteria while the American staff waited it out in boats on the river. Greg Grandin, whose book Fordlandia is the standard account, told NPR that the early years ran on waste, violence and vice, and that the right reference point is Deadwood rather than Thornton Wilder’s Our Town.Why Fordlandia failedWhat truly cracked the town was not the workers, it was the trees. Hevea brasiliensis does not grow in stands in the wild. It grows scattered, individual trees separated by other species, and that dispersal is the tree’s defence against a fungus it has co-evolved with over millennia. Planting them in tiny rows will have the defence stop working almost instantly.Ford’s trees went in close together on hilly, thin soil that the rains washed out from under them, and South American leaf blight moved through the plantings, along with saúva ants, lace bugs, red spiders and leaf caterpillars. A century of work on the pathogen, reviewed in the journal Plant Disease, treats the destruction of Ford’s two sites as the clearest demonstration of what the disease does to concentrated rubber.By 1933 the problem was obvious enough that Ford hired an actual plant pathologist, James Weir, who chose a fresh site about 130 kilometres downstream. Belterra was the more successful attempt. Weir brought back budwood from high-yielding Asian trees and set up a research nursery. The new manager relaxed the Dearborn-style rules and deferred to local custom on food and entertainment, and the town got schools, churches, a library, radio stations and a golf course. Brazil’s president visited in 1940 and called it a model community.Commercial tapping began in 1942 and produced 750 tons of latex. Ford’s factories needed 38,000 tons a year. Then the war ended, the Asian plantations reopened, synthetic rubber was established, and no argument remained for staying. Total investment had reached $20 million. Ford Motor Company sold both plantations to the Brazilian government for around $250,000, which Atlas Obscura notes is next to nothing compared to what went in.Ford had announced a grand tour of South America back in 1927, with Charles Lindbergh flying him down in the Spirit of St. Louis. The tour never happened. He never saw either town.The disease has still never reached Asia. More than 90 per cent of the world’s natural rubber grows there, on trees descended from a very narrow genetic base, and keeping the fungus out is permanent work. A pest risk analysis lodged with the FAO by Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, India, China, Vietnam and Sri Lanka sets out what that takes, down to steam cleaning secondhand chainsaws and logging machinery before they are shipped.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: BJD protests UPI changes, says Centre should fund digital payments
articles.summary: India News: The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) on Saturday rejected the Centre's decision to impose a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate (MDR) on person-to-merchant UPI t.
articles.body: The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) on Saturday rejected the Centre's decision to impose a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate (MDR) on person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, with Rajya Sabha MP Santrupt Misra saying the government should explore other ways to fund the digital-payment infrastructure.The charge will come into effect from October 15 and, according to Misra, could either cut merchants' profit margins or eventually be passed on to consumers.Misra said the government could have borne the cost of maintaining the UPI network instead of introducing the charge."In 2025-2026, the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) gave a dividend of Rs 2.86 lakh crore to the government. A small part of this could have been kept aside for the digital-transaction infrastructure," the Odisha MP said at a press conference at the Constitution Club here.He also pointed to the financial position of banks and platforms that are shareholders and promoters of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which operates UPI.BJD warns of impact on merchantsAccording to Misra, these banks made a combined profit of Rs 2.5 lakh crore last year and could have contributed a small portion towards maintaining digital-payment infrastructure.He rejected the government's position that the MDR would not affect consumers."The government says the MDR will not impact consumers. But this is a complete misunderstanding of economics," Misra said.The 0.4 per cent MDR will apply to UPI payments above Rs 2,000 made to merchants from October 15.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: India will take decisions in the best interests of its people and will continue to follow an independent foreign policy, minister of state for external affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh said while responding to a question on the Russian Sanctions Bill and its possible impact on India.“The people of India are the top priority for our government. We will take every measure that benefits our public,” Singh said while talking to ANI.‘We act in best interests of our country’Singh said India does not base its decisions on the dictates of other nations and will take steps to safeguard the country's strength and stability.“We will take decisive steps to ensure the strength and stability of our nation and its population. We maintain an independent foreign policy; we do not align ourselves based on the dictates of other nations but rather act in the best interests of our own country,” he said.He also reiterated India's position on the tariffs being imposed, saying, “We have consistently maintained that the tariffs being imposed are unfair, and we do not operate under pressure from any other nation.”Energy remains ‘primary concern’On India's energy needs, Singh said the government would continue to source energy based on what is commercially viable and economical.“Energy is a primary concern for us; we will source energy for our country and our people from wherever we find commercially viable and economical options,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia should respond to US sanctions with 'military deterrence': Dmitry Medvedev
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Russia should respond to new US sanctions with “military deterrence”, former president Dmitry Medvedev said on Saturday, without elaborating on what m.
articles.body: Russia should respond to new US sanctions with “military deterrence”, former president Dmitry Medvedev said on Saturday, without elaborating on what measures Moscow should consider.Medvedev, who is deputy chair of Russia’s Security Council and a senior ally of president Vladimir Putin, made the remarks on Telegram after US President Donald Trump signed a new sanctions law targeting Russia. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Friday. The White House said the law “authorizes and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran.”“Even across the ocean, they hear only the language of direct military deterrence, and that is the language in which we should respond to Russophobic atrocities, such as the law of the dead terrorist, Graham,” Medvedev said, referring to the legislation named after the late US Senator Lindsey Graham.The legislation targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, Russian officials, financial entities and the so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers used to evade sanctions. It also gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas.The US house of representatives passed the measure 262-159 on Wednesday, following Senate approval by 86-11 in August. The bill was championed by Graham, a Republican and longtime critic of Moscow, who died in July.The new measures come as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues into its fifth year. Russian officials, including Putin, have repeatedly accused Ukraine and Western countries supporting Kyiv of being involved in what Moscow describes as terrorist activity. Kyiv has rejected such accusations.The legislation also has implications for countries that continue to purchase Russian energy, including India and China. India on Friday reiterated that its energy sourcing decisions are guided by national interest, with MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal calling meeting the requirements of the country’s 1.4 billion people an “imperative”. Responding to questions on Russian oil purchases amid US pressure, Jaiswal said India buys energy from “diversified sources”. On the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act, he said India had conveyed concerns to senior US officials over its implications for energy security, international energy markets and the bilateral relationship.Medvedev, who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012 and later became deputy chair of the Security Council, has frequently criticised Western governments and Ukraine in public statements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Illinois issued the first permit for an $18 billion data-centre campus covering up to 472 acres; an 800,000-sq-ft first building moves ahead as neighbours say they learned too late to weigh in
articles.summary: US News: A massive data-centre campus planned in Grayslake, Illinois, has moved a step closer to construction after the village issued its first building permi.
articles.body: A massive data-centre campus planned in Grayslake, Illinois, has moved a step closer to construction after the village issued its first building permit, paving the way for an 800,000-square-foot facility. The larger development is expected to involve as much as $18 billion in private investment, but the project has also triggered opposition from residents who say they were not given a meaningful opportunity to weigh in before approvals were granted.The T5 Data Centres project, known as the Cornerstone development, is planned on land along Peterson Road in Grayslake. The latest plans call for about 6.7 million square feet of data-centre space to be built over 7 to 10 years. Earlier approvals allowed for a larger development of up to about 473 acres and as much as 10.1 million square feet, according to village documents. The village said the initial permit marks the operational start of the multibillion-dollar campus, with site work moving forward.Neighbours say they found out too lateWhile the village and developer have promoted the project as a major economic investment, some nearby residents say they were unaware of the scale of the development until after key approvals had already been granted.CBS Chicago reported that residents living close to the future data centre said they did not realise what was planned until the project had already been approved. Rob Baum, whose family has owned property near the site for three generations, said he had believed the land was simply farmland and was surprised by the scale of the planned construction."This was all farm field," he said. "My uncle owns like five acres back there. It seemed like they kinda snuck it under the table a little bit," Baum said.Hannah Harris, another resident, told CBS that residents did not understand that the project was being approved because of what she described as "ambiguous language." She said she began attending village meetings after learning more about the development, but by then the project had already received approval. The concerns extend beyond the size of the buildings. Residents have raised questions about potential environmental effects, water consumption, electricity demand, noise and wetlands around the site.The opposition has also moved into the legal arena. A lawsuit filed by opponents seeks to challenge the village's approvals, while residents have organised through the Lake County Data Centre Opposition Coalition. Earlier reporting by the Daily Herald said opponents argued that the public hearings surrounding the approvals were inadequate and that the village did not commission third-party studies to support some of its conclusions. Those are allegations made by opponents and remain subject to the legal process.What the village and T5 sayT5 Data Centres has defended the development and said it intends to continue engaging with residents. Pete Marin, CEO and chairman of T5, said the company was committed to incorporating community input. He pointed to the company's decision to voluntarily withdraw an application related to the remediation of local wetlands after hearing concerns from residents.T5 has also said it is working with the village on standards involving noise, water and electricity use. The company has said the project is expected to generate about $1.4 billion in property tax and permit-fee revenue over 20 years.The Village of Grayslake has similarly emphasised the financial impact. According to village officials, the project is moving forward without local tax incentives, exemptions or tax-increment financing subsidies. The village estimates the campus could generate approximately $1.4 billion in property tax revenue for local taxing bodies over its first 20 years.The village currently operates with a balanced budget and no municipal debt, officials said, meaning the additional revenue could potentially support infrastructure, parks, trails, schools and other community projects rather than being used to pay existing municipal debt.Water use, power and environmental questionsData centres have attracted increasing attention in the US because of their electricity and water requirements, particularly as artificial intelligence drives demand for computing capacity. Grayslake officials say the planned campus will use closed-loop cooling systems and estimate that an average data-centre building would consume around 2,500 to 3,500 gallons of water a day. For the full 6.75-million-square-foot campus, the village estimates total water use at approximately 50,000 gallons per day.The developer is also expected to fund the electrical infrastructure the campus requires, including an electrical substation on the property, according to the village.The village has stressed that the permit does not exempt the project from environmental or other regulatory requirements. The facilities will remain subject to local, state and federal rules covering issues including stormwater, sound, lighting, sewer discharges, air emissions and water use.Wetlands have nevertheless remained a point of contention. T5 previously sought permission to remediate isolated wetlands by replacing them elsewhere, but later withdrew that application after concerns were raised. The company has said the decision followed community feedback.A major development still facing scrutinyThe first 800,000-square-foot permit does not mean the entire campus will appear at once. The development is expected to unfold in phases over several years, with the latest plan envisioning multiple buildings and millions of square feet of data-centre space.The economic potential is therefore unfolding alongside questions over how the project was approved and how its environmental and infrastructure impacts will be managed.For Grayslake, the development represents a potentially major change to the local landscape and tax base. For nearby residents, the debate is also about how much say communities should have when large technology projects are planned in their neighbourhoods.As construction moves forward, the first building will provide an early indication of how the promises around water use, electricity infrastructure, environmental safeguards, noise and community engagement translate from plans into reality.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong: Has China gained access to US stealth tech?
articles.summary: International News: Sensitive components of the F-35 fighter jet were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the United States for repai.
articles.body: Sensitive components of the F-35 fighter jet were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the United States for repairs, prompting a US investigation and congressional briefings over the possibility that highly classified technology could have fallen within China's reach.The shipment was rerouted while crossing the Pacific, according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to Politico on condition of anonymity. The Pentagon has confirmed that some of the F-35 components went missing.The parts were being transported by an intermediary for F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin but ended up in Hong Kong. It remains unclear why the shipment was diverted or who currently has possession of the components.The incident, which had not previously been reported, prompted State Department and Pentagon officials to brief congressional staff working on key national security committees. The first briefings took place in June, with further meetings expected in the coming weeks, according to Politico.F-35 canopy raises security concernsThe shipment included an F-35 cockpit canopy, according to two people familiar with the matter. The canopy incorporates stealth technology available only to the US and its allies.An adversary with access to the component could potentially study it and attempt to reverse-engineer aspects of the technology.The Pentagon's F-35 Joint Program Office said it was "aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components".The office said it was working with US authorities and industry partners "to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence".J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staff member and Congressional Research Service military aviation analyst, told Politico that China has sought F-35 data through espionage.Even if China already possessed technical specifications or other information about the components, Gertler said, access to an actual part could help verify or refine what it had obtained.Hong Kong diversion puts supply chain under scrutinyThe diversion to Hong Kong has raised concerns because the city is a special administrative region of China and Beijing has tightened its control over Hong Kong in recent years.The F-35 programme relies on a vast international supply chain involving the US and allied countries including the UK, Australia, Denmark, Norway and Poland. Lockheed Martin manages the programme's overall supply chain and uses commercial shipping providers to move components.Australia has maintenance facilities for F-35s, but none is currently equipped to repair the aircraft's canopies, according to Politico.The canopy is an acrylic cockpit enclosure coated with a thin layer of transparent radar-absorbent material designed to reduce the aircraft's visibility to enemy radar. The coating can degrade over time, requiring canopies to be repaired or replaced.Lockheed Martin said it could not discuss individual shipments for security reasons but follows US regulations governing the transportation of aircraft components."Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 program and the security of our allied partners," the company said.The State Department declined to comment on the report to Politico, while the Chinese embassy said it was not familiar with the incident.The episode has also drawn attention to longstanding concerns over F-35 spare-parts tracking. A 2023 government accountability office report found that more than one million F-35 spare parts had gone missing over a five-year period and said the Pentagon lacked adequate visibility into some losses because Lockheed Martin maintained the relevant records.The F-35 programme has also faced continuing concerns over spare-parts shortages and rising sustainment costs. The Pentagon expects the programme to cost nearly $2 trillion over its lifetime.

articles.title: Indian truck driver arrested in Utah months after fatal California hit-and-run that killed 2
articles.summary: US News: Chamkaur Singh, an Indian truck driver, was arrested in Utah for a fatal California hit-and-run that left two dead. Police discovered a homicide warrant during a routine traffic stop, leading to his arrest months after the incident.
articles.body: An Indian truck driver wanted in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in California was arrested in Utah months after the crash, when police stopped him for speeding and discovered a warrant linked to the deaths of two people.Chamkaur Singh, 30, was pulled over by police in Moab, Utah, on September 1 while driving a semi-truck. During the traffic stop, officers found a nationwide warrant from California charging him with homicide-vehicular manslaughter, Dailywire reported.The warrant was linked to a March 29 crash in Ontario, California, in which seven vehicles were involved. California Highway Patrol officers were responding to an earlier two-vehicle collision when a semi-truck travelling in the slow lane rear-ended a car, killing one passenger and critically injuring another.The truck then struck another vehicle, killing a second person. Two other people were also injured in the pile-up.Singh allegedly fled the scene after the crash. He was arrested without incident in Moab and booked into the Grand County Jail. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer against him the following day.California issued Singh a commercial driver’s licence (CDL) on May 10, 2025, according to DHS. The department said the licence remains active despite three convictions on his driving record for improper lane or location, following too closely and speeding.Singh had already received a deportation order when his CDL was issued.According to the department, Singh said he left India in December 2020 and travelled through the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Panama, Honduras, Guatemala and Mexico before entering the US through Arizona in August 2021.He was then arrested by US Border Patrol after entering the country but was later released, DHS said.DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticised the circumstances surrounding Singh’s release and the issuance of his commercial driving licence.“This illegal alien from India is accused of causing a semi-truck crash that killed two people in California,” Mullin said. “Despite having three convictions on his driving record, his CDL is still active.”Mullin also criticised the Biden administration’s immigration policies and California Governor Gavin Newsom’s policies, calling for changes to what DHS described as sanctuary policies.Singh remains in custody in Utah over the California warrant.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
